title: Customize the player UI
lead: Start by comparing an existing theme and its applied UI settings in the Web app. Use the matching factory and stylesheet when carrying that change into your own player. This chapter separates GUI experiments from changes that require editing code.

blocks.text: Choose a starting point

rows: Use Default (Bitmovin) in the app. For an independent app needing the SDK's complete responsive variant selection, use UIFactory.buildUI from bitmovin-player-ui.
Add a class to the standard tree and style it with CSS or SCSS. Neon is one example.
Recompose the component arrays in UIContainer and ControlBar.
Extend Label, Button or ToggleButton. Scores and live wall-clock labels are examples.

blocks.text: UIManager connects the player and UI. UIContainer is the root of the displayed components; ControlBar holds playback controls; Container arranges components. Spacer expands the gap between them. Keeping these roles separate helps distinguish appearance changes from playback-engine configuration.
Follow a GUI change into code

items: Select Premiere and keep the same VOD source playing. Open its settings gear and locate the playback-speed selector.
Turn Speed item in settings gear off in UI settings. Reopen the gear and confirm that the item is absent; turn it on and check that it returns.
Expand Applied UIConfig overrides beside the video. The playbackSpeedSelectionEnabled value reflects the change. The theme construction example above it still describes the component tree.

Use the factory path below Construction code to inspect buildPremiereUiContainer and buildSettingsPanel in liveUi.ts. PlaybackSpeedSelectBox is the component that the flag controls; changing its position requires editing that component tree.

blocks.text: The app's DefaultUIFactory wraps the standard desktop/main component tree to expose autohide. It does not reproduce all small-screen, TV, advertising and empty-state variants supplied by UIFactory.buildUI. CSS themes use the same wrapper. Compare them as this app's desktop UI examples.
Create and release a UI

This TypeScript example runs inside the repository workspace, where @showcase/ui-shared and its compiled CSS are available. Pass the player element and your Player license to createPlayerWithUi, then load your SourceConfig with the returned player.load(). Calling usePremiere replaces only the UI, and release removes the UI before destroying the player. The flag shown matches the GUI experiment above; setting it to true restores the speed selector.
Change appearance with CSS

Neon adds a class while retaining the Default component tree. The factory call below is the same approach used by the app. The imported shared stylesheet already contains the skin; use its rules as the starting point when editing your own colors.

The corresponding seek-bar rule is in ui-shared.scss. The UI library adds the bmpui- prefix to component classes, which explains the class names used by CSS. Load overrides after the base stylesheet and scope them to the skin class so that other themes are unaffected.
Change the component layout

This executable excerpt follows the Compact tree, omitting its optional casting buttons. The order inside components determines the controls in the row. Move PlaybackTimeLabel before SeekBar to compare the arrangement. There is no component-order editor in the GUI; edit and rebuild the code, then compare the result with Compact in the app.

Create fresh components for each UIManager. Release the previous manager before attaching this UI to a player created with ui: false. This compact example deliberately has no central play overlay, volume controls, settings menu or subtitle overlay; choose the corresponding components from another factory if your application needs them.
Reuse the result in your application

items: Choose whether you need only CSS, a different component tree or a new component. Keep player loading and playback configuration separate from UI construction.
For a project in this workspace, import the required factory and @showcase/ui-shared/css. @showcase/ui-shared is a private workspace package, not a package published for npm installation.

For an independent project, install bitmovin-player and bitmovin-player-ui with the versions used by this repository as a reference. Import bitmovin-player-ui/dist/css/bitmovinplayer-ui.css, then copy or adapt the required factory, custom components and skin rules with their license notices. App-specific names such as PremiereUIFactory are defined in this repository, not in the SDK.

Transfer the applied UIConfig values and the separate factory options such as hideDelay. If the theme needs recommendations, markers or playlist callbacks, supply those from your own application; the construction example does not export that app data.
Compare playback, keyboard focus, fullscreen, source changes and repeated UI replacement. Restore the previous UI or release the UI and destroy the player when leaving the screen.

blocks.text: Selecting a theme in the app retains UIConfig overrides. When testing a modification, restore each changed setting or reload the app before comparing. Browser-stored playback preferences and resume positions may remain. The UI settings chapter explains which media and components each setting needs.

blocks.text: Common UI modifications

items: Add or remove a control by editing the ControlBar component array.
Keep controls visible by setting UIContainer hideDelay to -1.
Recolor one element by checking its target class and CSS specificity.
Show title and description with TitleBar and SourceConfig values.
Show the next videos using RecommendationOverlay and metadata.recommendations.
Create a label that follows a player value by extending Label and updating it from events.

blocks.text: Hide custom labels

Label.hide() adds the bmpui-hidden class. In UI 4.23.0, the standard label's hidden style is scoped to its ui-label class. Setting cssClass replaces that base class, so a custom label needs a matching hidden style. Use cssClasses to add styling classes while retaining the base class, or include an explicit rule when replacing it. The shared stylesheet includes this rule for WallClockLabel and BehindLiveLabel.

Test the transition from live to on-demand playback after the clock has displayed text. A label that is empty on a fresh on-demand source can have zero height even when its hidden style is missing. Check retained clock text, the hidden class, actual CSS display and showing the label again. This stylesheet is used by the Web app, custom UIs on iOS and Android, and both React Native hosts. tvOS uses native System UI and Vega uses Kepler controls.
Release custom components

Call super.configure from configure and subscribe to playback events to update the display. Release timers, event subscriptions and auxiliary components from their owning component release method. Removing a UI from the screen alone does not establish that its resources have been released, particularly with repeated theme changes.

The shared UI package also includes cleanup fixes for auxiliary objects in the pinned UI library. When adapting a component, keep its release handling with its event subscriptions and timers; otherwise theme replacement can leave work running after the UI has disappeared.

Guide examples such as UIVariant, TV SpatialNavigation and VR do not mean that every corresponding control is implemented in the current Web app. Distinguish GUI controls, examples requiring code changes and capabilities requiring physical devices.
